title: The Truth About Stockholm Syndrome
summary: Stockholm syndrome describes hostages bonding with captors, but psychologists view the evidence as dubious and it is not in the DSM.
evidenceNote: Stockholm syndrome has never been included in the DSM-5. Psychologists generally consider evidence for the condition to be dubious or nonexistent, with many foundational details from the 1973 bank robbery either partly or entirely fabricated.

scenes.text: What if a famous psychological disorder was actually invented by someone who never even met the victims?
emphasis: invented by someone who never even met the victims

scenes.text: The term stems from a 1973 bank robbery in Stockholm where four employees were held captive for six days in a bank vault.
Criminologist Nils Bejerot coined the term after the bank robbery, despite never speaking to the hostages.
emphasis: never spoke to or met the hostages

scenes.text: Hostage Kristin Enmark later explained she was merely trying to survive, and actually feared police incompetence more than the robbers.

items.title: Survival Mode
items.detail: Doing what it takes to stay alive during the ordeal.

items.title: Police Fear
items.detail: Hostages felt police actions posed a direct threat to their lives.

scenes.text: Is Stockholm syndrome an official psychiatric diagnosis?
scenes.answer: No. It has never been included in the DSM, and psychologists consider evidence for it to be dubious.
emphasis: never been included in the DSM-5

scenes.text: Pop psychology often turns survival tactics and media hype into medical facts.
